stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, heaven on earth, and the flight north
stops.campa: In the summer of 1871 Morris takes the lease of a grey gabled Elizabethan manor by the young Thames near Lechlade: Kelmscott, which he calls heaven on earth, a house grown up out of the soil and the lives of those who lived on it. He takes it jointly, in a strange bitter arrangement, with Rossetti, who loves Jane; and then, as if fleeing his own house of grief, Morris turns his back on it within weeks and sails for Iceland. The old walls, the barn, the roses and the tapestried rooms will hold him at the last, but first he must go to the world's cold edge.
stops.quote: a heaven on earth; an old stone Elizabethan house... and such a garden! close down on the river, a boat house and all things handy.

stops.name: The Faroes and the first sight of Iceland, out of the world
stops.campa: The Diana beats north through the grey Atlantic and puts in among the Faroe Islands, black cliffs walling green shelves of turf where the little wooden town of Thorshavn clings above the sea. Morris, a plump prosperous Englishman leaving comfort behind, feels the ordinary world drop away; he writes of the strange solemn beauty, the sense of sailing off the edge of the known. Then on the thirteenth the long coast of Iceland lifts out of the water: the ice-mountain Vatnajökull hanging pale above the black shore, the land of the sagas rising, at last, real before his eyes.
stops.quote: the whole thing was rather solemn than beautiful... I felt as if some old chapter of the Sagas were opening before me.

stops.name: Reykjavík, landfall in the saga-land
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of July the mail-steamer Diana brings him into Reykjavík. With him ride his Icelandic co-translator Eiríkr Magnússon, his old Oxford friend Charles Faulkner, and young Evans; before them a train of ponies and the whole map of the Family Sagas he has taught himself to read in the original tongue. He steps ashore into a treeless grey world under enormous light and calls it, in his journal, our pilgrimage. The sagas he has Englished are no longer books to him; he has come to walk their ground and stand where their dead men fell.
stops.quote: the glorious simplicity of the terrible & tragic, but beautiful land with its well remembered stories of brave men... came upon me with a great shock.

stops.name: Þingvellir, the floor whose tomb is time past
stops.campa: They ride to Þingvellir, the rift-valley where for a thousand years the Icelanders met in open parliament, the Althing, upon the Law-Rock between the sundered walls of the earth. Here Njáll spoke and Gunnar was outlawed; here the whole nation once turned Christian in a day. Morris stands in the cleft of the black lava with the great lake beyond and feels the weight of dead law and dead speech under his feet. This is the grey minster of lands whose floor is the tomb of time past. The phrase will come to him among these stones.
stops.quote: Ye who have come o'er the sea to behold this grey minster of lands, / Whose floor is the tomb of time past, and whose walls by the toil of dead hands / Show pictures amidst of the ruin of deeds that have overpast death.
stops.quote_source: Morris, 'Gunnar's Howe above the House at Lithend', Poems by the Way (written after 1871)

stops.name: Bergþórshvoll, the burning of Njáll
stops.campa: Across the flat marsh-lands of Rangárvellir he rides to Bergþórshvoll, the low knoll where the wise Njáll and his sons were burned alive in their hall by their enemies, and where Njáll's wife Bergthóra would not come out but lay down with her husband under an ox-hide to die. Morris stands on the grassy mound with the sea-wind over it and the story alive in him as fact: he can all but smell the smoke. Of all the saga-sites this moves him most: the tragic, terrible, beautiful land, and the courage of men and women who chose their deaths without complaint.
stops.quote: I know how to answer thee well: I will not go out, for I am old, and little fit to avenge my sons, and I will not live in shame.
stops.quote_source: Njáls saga, ch. 129 (the burning), which Morris knew in the original

stops.name: Hlíðarendi, Gunnar's howe above the house at Lithend
stops.campa: He climbs to Hlíðarendi in the green Fljótshlíð, the home of Gunnar the archer, greatest of Njáll's friends. Here, riding into outlawry, Gunnar's horse stumbled and he turned and looked back at the slope of his home and said the fair hillside had never seemed so fair, and would not go, and stayed, and was killed. Above the house stands the howe, his grave-mound, where legend says he was seen singing merrily in the moonlight after death. Morris stands on the fragrant hayfield slope and understands the man who could not leave his own land, being himself such a man.
stops.quote: Fair is the Lithe; so fair that it has never seemed to me so fair; the corn fields are white to harvest, and the home mead is mown; and now I will ride back home, and not fare abroad at all.
stops.quote_source: Gunnar at Hlíðarendi, Njáls saga ch. 75 (Dasent's rendering, close to Morris's)

stops.name: Geysir and the desert of lava, the volcanic desolation
stops.campa: They come to the great Geysir, the spouting hot spring that gives its name to all such the world over, and camp on the sinter among the steam and the sulphur. Beyond lie the interior deserts: vast fields of black lava and grey ash, glaciers hanging over them, rivers to be forded that could drown a man and his pony together. Morris, the lover of green England, is undone and remade by this desolation. The saga-land's harshness teaches him what abundance costs; the socialism to come is seeded here, among a poor people living nobly on a hard earth.
stops.quote: the most romantic of all deserts... I think I was never so much moved by anything so little to be caught hold of.

stops.name: The second pilgrimage, Grettir's country and Sigurd Englished
stops.campa: In 1873 he returns, riding the northern quarter, the country of Grettir the Strong and of the Laxdæla folk, Bjarg where Grettir was born and the fells where he was hunted for twenty years. Out of these two journeys and his labour with Magnússon comes the great work: Sigurd the Volsung, the tale of the Northern Achilles and the cursed gold and the dragon Fáfnir, Englished into a rolling epic Morris holds the best thing he ever made. The North has given him a sterner music than the Earthly Paradise, and a myth of doom that will outlast his idle-singer days.
stops.quote: This is the Great Story of the North, which should be to all our race what the Tale of Troy was to the Greeks.
stops.quote_source: Morris, preface note to The Story of Sigurd the Volsung (1876)

stops.name: Queen Square, the wallpapers and the willow bough
stops.campa: Through the earlier seventies, from the workrooms at Queen Square, Morris the pattern-maker comes into his full power. He draws the wallpapers that will hang in half the houses of the world: Trellis with its little birds, Daisy, Pimpernel, and later Willow Bough, the acanthus and pomegranate scrolls, always from the living English hedge and garden, never a dead motif copied from a book. He preaches that the lesser arts, the papers and pots and hangings a man lives among, are the true measure of a civilisation's health, and that no work is worth making unless the maker took joy in the making of it.
stops.quote: If you want a golden rule that will fit everything, this is it: Have nothing in your houses that you do not know to be useful, or believe to be beautiful.
stops.quote_source: Morris, 'The Beauty of Life', lecture at Birmingham, 19 February 1880

stops.name: The Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings, Anti-Scrape
stops.campa: Enraged by the 'restorers' who scrape the honest age off old churches and rebuild them into lifeless copies, Morris founds the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings, which the trade nicknames Anti-Scrape. Old buildings, he argues, are not ours to falsify; they belong to all the generations that made them and to those not yet born; we are only trustees. It is the first true conservation movement, and its manifesto, in his own hot prose, still governs the care of monuments. The medievalist has become the guardian of the actual medieval stone.
stops.quote: These buildings do not belong to us only... they have belonged to our forefathers, and they will belong to our descendants unless we play them false. They are not in any sense our property, to do as we like with.

stops.name: Merton Abbey Works, on the Wandle, the blue vats and the loom
stops.campa: In June Morris moves the works to Merton Abbey on the river Wandle, seven acres of low sheds among willows and poplar-lined water. Here at last he has room for everything: the great indigo vats sunk in the ground, into which the cloth goes green and comes up, in the air, the true blue that eluded all the age; the high-warp tapestry looms; the stained-glass shop above the dye-house. He dyes with his own blue-stained hands, hunting out the old madder and weld and woad recipes the factories had thrown away. Art, he says, is man's expression of his joy in labour. And here he proves it.
stops.quote: Art is man's expression of his joy in labour.
stops.quote_source: Morris, 'Art under Plutocracy' / 'The Art of the People', lectures (early 1880s)

stops.name: The tapestry loom, the Adoration and the Holy Grail
stops.campa: At Merton the high-warp looms carry the crown of the Firm's work: great arras tapestries woven the old slow way, thread by thread from the back, after cartoons by Burne-Jones with foregrounds of flowers and scrolling acanthus by Morris and Dearle. The Adoration of the Magi goes to the Oxford chapel; the Quest of the Holy Grail, the largest of all, unrolls the whole Arthurian dream of his boyhood in wool and silk. The armour of the toy knight in Epping Forest has become a wall of woven knights; the medieval revelation of Oxford is made, at last, a thing the hands can weave.
stops.quote: the noblest of the weaving arts... in which we may reasonably imitate the earlier work of the Middle Ages.
stops.quote_source: Morris, on tapestry ('Textiles', Arts and Crafts Essays)
